modalities.name: Long Settle Imagery
modalities.tagline: Deep calm first, then one slow scene of being cared for.
modalities.whatItIs: Long Settle Imagery is a new, untested idea that pushes ideal parent imagery (picturing yourself as a child cared for by invented, ideal parents) further toward calm and absorption than the original method. A trained therapist spends most of a long session helping you settle deeply, then guides one slow, unchanging scene of being cared for, instead of exploring or talking with different sides of yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that care might sink in more fully when you are deeply settled and simply receiving, so the session spends its time on settling and receiving rather than on talking or exploring.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 90-minute session, the therapist guides about 40 minutes of slow settling through the breath, a body scan and a gradual quieting of thought. Then comes a single, carefully paced scene in which ideal parents protect, soothe and delight in the child you imagine being, followed by a slow return and a short talk about what stayed with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with lasting insecurity in close relationships who find that talk-heavy therapy keeps them in their heads, and who settle well with guided relaxation.
modalities.cautions: Deep calm can lower defenses, so painful memories of your real childhood may surface, and long relaxation can blur imagination and memory; it should be done only with a licensed therapist experienced in childhood trauma who keeps the scene clearly imagined. People prone to dissociation should avoid long relaxation inductions, and it is not a replacement for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Long Settle Imagery. A therapist spends most of the session helping you sink into deep calm, then guides one slow scene of being cared for by imagined ideal parents. For people whose minds stay busy in talk therapy. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: The Wordless Cradle
modalities.tagline: Imagined care from the time before you had words.
modalities.whatItIs: The Wordless Cradle is a proposed practice that takes ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, back to the earliest part of life, before language. Instead of scenes with conversations, you imagine being a baby who is held, rocked, fed and kept warm by ideal parents, and you mostly notice how that care feels in your body.
modalities.coreIdea: The first lessons about whether care can be relied on are learned before words, so this practice works with wordless, bodily images of being held rather than with talk, agendas or structured steps.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lying or reclining under a blanket, you follow a therapist's slow, sparse descriptions of being held close, rocked and warmed, with long quiet pauses in between. There is no goal to reach and little talking; at the end you describe in a few words what you felt, and the therapist checks how settled you are before you leave.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who sense that their insecurity runs deeper than any memory and who find that words get in the way of feeling cared for.
modalities.cautions: Imagining infancy can bring up strong, hard-to-name feelings of longing or grief and can feel very exposing, so it belongs only in ongoing therapy with a clinician who knows attachment work and keeps the pace slow. It must never be used to 'recover' memories from infancy, and it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: An idea: The Wordless Cradle. With a trained therapist you imagine being a baby who is held, rocked and kept warm by ideal parents, with almost no talking. For adults whose insecurity feels older than words. Untested, and only with a trauma-aware guide.

modalities.name: One Age at a Time
modalities.tagline: Ideal parent imagery as a planned journey through childhood.
modalities.whatItIs: One Age at a Time is a new, untested idea that turns ideal parent imagery into a planned journey through childhood, from toddler to teenager. Each block of sessions imagines ideal parents meeting the needs of one age, such as a five-year-old's fears at night or a teenager's need for both freedom and limits.
modalities.coreIdea: Children need different kinds of care at different ages, so this practice offers imagined care stage by stage, rather than as one general scene, and moves on only when an age feels settled.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a trained therapist first choose about six ages to visit, from around two to sixteen. Over several weekly sessions per age, the therapist guides scenes of ideal parents caring for you at that age, and you move on to the next age only when the current one feels settled to you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who notice that their struggles in relationships feel tied to particular stages, such as early school years or adolescence, and who like a clear long-term plan.
modalities.cautions: Moving through the years can stir up memories of what really happened at each age, so this is only for work with a trauma-informed therapist who keeps imagined scenes separate from memories. It is long-term work with no evidence behind it yet, and it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: One Age at a Time. Ideal parent imagery as a planned journey through childhood, one age per block of sessions, from toddler to teen, each with the care that age needed. For adults who feel stuck at one stage. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Tucked In Imagery
modalities.tagline: Comfort only: an imagined bedtime with parents who stay.
modalities.whatItIs: Tucked In Imagery is a gentle, speculative variation on ideal parent imagery that stays entirely on soothing, with no searching for what hurts or why. Each session imagines one ordinary bedtime: ideal parents settling the child you picture being, staying close and leaving a light on, until the scene ends in safe, sleepy calm.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people may need to feel soothed many times before they can safely look at anything painful, so this practice offers comfort only and never goes digging.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie or recline in a dim, quiet room while the therapist guides a 20-minute bedtime scene: a bath, a story, a tucking in, and parents who stay until you feel drowsy. Afterwards you rest for a few minutes, sit up slowly and talk briefly about how calm you feel, rather than about the past.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel on edge most of the time, find bedtime or being alone at night hard, and want a gentle way in before any deeper work.
modalities.cautions: Even soothing scenes can awaken grief for the care you missed, so it should still happen only within therapy led by a clinician experienced in attachment work, and any other care you receive should continue. Deep relaxation can leave some people drowsy or spacey, so take a few minutes before driving.
modalities.tweet: What if therapy began with being tucked in? Tucked In Imagery is a new idea: a therapist guides a calm bedtime scene where ideal parents settle the child you picture being, with no digging into the past. For people who rarely feel safe enough to rest.

modalities.name: Overheard Kindness
modalities.tagline: Imagining ideal parents speaking warmly about you, out of earshot.
modalities.whatItIs: Overheard Kindness is a proposed variation on ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, that works only through words, with no body work at all. Instead of being spoken to directly, the child you picture being overhears the ideal parents talking warmly about them in the next room, when they think no one is listening.
modalities.coreIdea: Praise said to your face can feel like politeness, but kind words overheard are harder to dismiss, so the practice delivers care as something the parents say when they have nothing to gain.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a therapist guides you to picture yourself as a child in bed or on the stairs, hearing the ideal parents talk about your day, what they noticed and what they love about you. The therapist voices both parents in slow, ordinary sentences, and afterwards you note which overheard line stayed with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who brush off compliments, suspect kindness has a motive, or grew up overhearing criticism rather than warmth.
modalities.cautions: Overhearing scenes can echo memories of overhearing arguments or harsh talk, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist experienced in childhood trauma who keeps the scenes clearly invented. It is untested and should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Overheard Kindness. In guided imagery, the child you once were overhears imagined ideal parents in the next room talking warmly about you when they think you can't hear. For people who brush off compliments. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Lessons From Ideal Parents
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who teach the life skills nobody taught you.
modalities.whatItIs: Lessons From Ideal Parents is an experimental extension of ideal parent imagery in which the imagined parents do more than comfort: they teach. Where gentler methods wait to see what arises, the therapist plans each scene around one skill a child needs, such as calming down after anger, asking for help or losing a game gracefully, and the ideal parents show it patiently.
modalities.coreIdea: Many adults lack skills that are normally passed on in childhood, so this practice lets them be learned inside an imagined relationship of warmth and patience.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each block of sessions, you and the therapist choose one skill and plan a short series of scenes in which ideal parents model it, coach the child you picture being and celebrate small tries. You end each session by naming one way to practice the same skill in your adult life that week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel they missed basic emotional lessons growing up, such as how to handle frustration or ask for comfort.
modalities.cautions: Scenes about missing lessons can stir up grief or shame about your real upbringing, so this belongs only within therapy led by a clinician trained in attachment and trauma care. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Lessons From Ideal Parents. Guided imagery where invented ideal parents patiently teach the child you once were the skills nobody taught you, like calming down or asking for help. For adults who missed those lessons. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: The Five Gifts Course
modalities.tagline: One structured module for each quality of secure care.
modalities.whatItIs: The Five Gifts Course would turn ideal parent imagery into a structured program with one module for each quality of secure care: protection, soothing, being understood, encouragement to explore, and delight. Each module has set scenes, home recordings and simple ratings, so progress is planned and visible rather than left to unfold on its own.
modalities.coreIdea: Building each quality of felt security on purpose, one at a time, might make the work easier to follow and to track than open-ended sessions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about 15 weekly sessions, three per quality, a trained therapist guides a scripted scene focused on that module's gift and gives you a short recording to use at home. At the start and end of each module you rate statements such as 'I can be comforted' from 0 to 10, and the therapist slows the pace if a module stirs up too much.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with insecure attachment who like clear structure, measurable steps and knowing what comes next.
modalities.cautions: Set steps can feel pressured when old pain surfaces, so it should run only with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care who is free to slow down or stop. The ratings are a guide rather than proof, and the course is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who like structure: The Five Gifts Course. Ideal parent imagery as a planned program, one module each for protection, soothing, being understood, encouragement and delight, with simple ratings to track how it feels. Untested, therapist-led.

modalities.name: Twin Guide Intensive
modalities.tagline: A few planned days of imagery, with two practitioners present.
modalities.whatItIs: Twin Guide Intensive is an untested concept that runs ideal parent imagery as a concentrated block of sessions over a few days, with every minute planned. Two trained practitioners work together: one voices and guides the imagery while the other watches your breathing and posture, tracks your comfort and calls pauses.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentrated, carefully planned time with imagined care might build momentum that weekly sessions lose between visits, and a second practitioner makes that intensity safer to hold.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over three to five days you have two or three planned sessions a day, each with a short settling, a scripted scene and a structured debrief, plus rest breaks and meals at set times. Both practitioners meet you before and after the block to agree on stop signals and to plan follow-up with your regular therapist.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults already in therapy for attachment difficulties who feel that weekly sessions lose momentum and who can take a few days away from daily demands.
modalities.cautions: Intensive formats can stir up a lot quickly, so this is only for people screened as stable enough, with two practitioners experienced in attachment and trauma care, clear stop signals and planned aftercare. It is not suitable during a crisis, and it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Twin Guide Intensive. A few days of planned ideal parent imagery, where one practitioner guides the scenes and a second watches your comfort and calls pauses. For people in therapy who feel weekly sessions lose momentum. Not for a crisis.

modalities.name: Known in Detail
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who know the small, particular facts of you.
modalities.whatItIs: Known in Detail is an untested idea that turns ideal parent imagery away from general, all-embracing goodwill and toward particular knowledge. The imagined ideal parents know the child you picture being in fine detail: the stuffed toy you sleep with, the joke that makes you laugh, the food you refuse, the worry you have not mentioned yet.
modalities.coreIdea: Kindness wished to everyone can feel impersonal, so this practice builds the experience of being cared for by someone who knows you specifically and remembers.
modalities.whatYouDo: In early sessions, you and a trained therapist list small, harmless details about who you were as a child, such as likes, habits and fears, without going into painful history. Later sessions guide scenes in which the ideal parents notice and use those details, remembering a favorite song on a hard day or knowing what you need before you ask.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel interchangeable, unseen in their particulars, or loved only in general terms.
modalities.cautions: Listing childhood details can lead toward painful memories, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist who knows attachment and trauma work and keeps the imagined parents clearly separate from real ones. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Known in Detail. Guided imagery where ideal parents know the small facts of the child you were: the toy you slept with, the joke that made you laugh. For people who feel loved only in general terms. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: They Come Back
modalities.tagline: Imagined goodbyes that always end in a reunion.
modalities.whatItIs: They Come Back is an untested concept built on the part of secure attachment that is about time: trusting that care continues while someone is out of sight. In guided imagery, ideal parents leave for short, clearly explained absences and always return, and the scenes stretch those separations gradually.
modalities.coreIdea: Where insight meditation shows that every experience passes, this practice does the opposite and builds a felt sense that a caring bond lasts through absence and change.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist guides scenes in which ideal parents say goodbye, explain when they will be back and return on time, starting with a few minutes in the next room and building up to a night away. Each scene ends with the reunion, and between sessions you can listen to a short recording of a return before a separation that worries you, such as a partner's trip.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who panic when someone close is away or slow to reply, or who expect every goodbye to be the last.
modalities.cautions: Scenes of separation can stir up real memories of abandonment, so this is only for work with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care who builds the steps slowly. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments for anxiety or trauma.
modalities.tweet: Experimental concept: They Come Back. Guided imagery where ideal parents leave for short, explained absences and always return, with the gaps growing slowly. For people who panic when someone close is away or slow to reply. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: All Afternoon for You
modalities.tagline: Imagined time with parents who have nowhere else to be.
modalities.whatItIs: All Afternoon for You is a speculative idea that pushes ideal parent imagery toward complete rest and open time, the opposite of anything timed or intense. Each session imagines a long, lazy afternoon in which ideal parents have nowhere else to be, ask nothing of the child you picture being and simply enjoy the time together.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people learned that attention had to be earned or squeezed in, so this practice offers imagined time with no clock, no tasks and nothing to prove.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting or lying comfortably, you follow a therapist's loose, slow guidance into a scene such as a quiet afternoon at home, with fewer set steps than usual and plenty of silence. You are free to let the scene drift, and the session ends with a few minutes of noticing how it feels to have had someone's time without asking for it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who always feel rushed, feel like a burden on other people's time, or believe they must perform to be wanted.
modalities.cautions: Loosely guided imagery can drift toward painful memories or leave some people drowsy or spacey, so it should be practiced only with a clinician experienced in attachment work, who checks in often. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: A thought experiment: what if someone had nowhere else to be but with you? All Afternoon for You is guided imagery where ideal parents ask nothing, rush nowhere and simply enjoy your company. For people who feel like a burden on others' time. Untested idea.

modalities.name: Held in Solitude
modalities.tagline: Learning to be alone while still feeling cared for.
modalities.whatItIs: Held in Solitude is a thought experiment that uses ideal parent imagery to practice being alone without feeling abandoned. After guided sessions that build a scene of ideal parents, you spend stretches of quiet time by yourself, sensing that the imagined care stays with you even when no one is there.
modalities.coreIdea: A secure child can play happily alone because a caring presence feels close inside, so this practice trains that inner company directly, in solitude rather than with other people.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session begins with a therapist guiding a short scene of ideal parents, then you sit alone in a quiet room for 20 to 40 minutes, with the therapist nearby and a simple way to call them. Afterwards you meet briefly to talk about when the inner company felt near or far, and the alone time grows slowly over the weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find being alone frightening or empty, and who fill every quiet moment with screens, noise or other people.
modalities.cautions: Time alone can bring up loneliness or old fears of abandonment, so it is only for use inside therapy with a clinician experienced in childhood trauma, the steps must stay small, the therapist must stay within reach, and anyone at risk of self-harm should not use solitude practice. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For people who find being alone frightening, a new idea: Held in Solitude. A therapist helps you build imagery of ideal parents, then you practice short stretches of quiet time alone, sensing the care stays with you. Untested, built up in small steps.

modalities.name: Little and Often Visits
modalities.tagline: Short, frequent scenes of care instead of long sessions.
modalities.whatItIs: Little and Often Visits proposes delivering ideal parent imagery, the practice of picturing care from invented ideal parents, in very short, frequent sessions instead of long ones. A trained therapist guides brief, tightly structured scenes of about ten minutes, several times a week, so the experience of being cared for comes back often, the way a young child is checked on through the day.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure care is built from many small, reliable moments rather than a few long ones, so in this practice frequency matters more than length or stamina.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three or four times a week you meet a therapist, in person or by video, for a 15-minute slot: a minute to settle, about ten minutes of one scripted scene and a quick check of how you feel. Scenes repeat with small variations, and once a month a longer session reviews how it is going.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find long sessions draining or hard to fit in, or whose sense of being cared for fades quickly between weekly visits.
modalities.cautions: Short slots leave little time to settle if something painful comes up, so it should run only with a trauma-informed therapist who has a plan for a longer follow-up when needed. There is no evidence for it yet, so it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Little and often, the way a child is checked on all day: the idea behind Little and Often Visits. A therapist guides a ten-minute scene of imagined ideal parents several times a week. For people whose sense of care fades fast. Untested.

modalities.name: Carried for a While
modalities.tagline: Imagery for practicing being helped instead of being strong.
modalities.whatItIs: Carried for a While is an untested concept that uses ideal parent imagery to practice being helped rather than being strong. The scenes picture ideal parents carrying the child, taking the heavy bags, sorting out the problem and letting the child lean on them completely, with no expectation of coping alone.
modalities.coreIdea: People who had to grow up fast may never have felt what it is like to depend on someone, so this practice makes imagined dependence, rather than effort or self-reliance, the main experience.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a trained therapist guides slow, loosely structured scenes of being carried, looked after when ill, or having a grown-up take over a task that was too much. You notice any urge to take back control, let the imagined parents keep carrying, and end by naming one small way you might accept help this week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who are always the strong one, find it very hard to ask for help, and feel uneasy when others look after them.
modalities.cautions: Letting yourself lean, even in imagination, can bring up grief about having had to cope alone, so use it only within therapy led by a clinician experienced in attachment and trauma. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For everyone who is always the strong one, an idea: Carried for a While. Guided imagery where ideal parents carry the load and let the child you once were lean on them completely. A way to practice being helped. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Imagined Home
modalities.tagline: Designing, then visiting, the calm household you never had.
modalities.whatItIs: The Imagined Home is a proposed extension of ideal parent imagery that builds not only the ideal parents but the whole household they keep: the rooms, the meals, the rules and the daily rhythm. Over many sessions you and a therapist design this home in detail, then spend guided time living ordinary days in it.
modalities.coreIdea: Security grows from a predictable everyday world as much as from single moments of comfort, so this practice gives that world a lasting, structured shape in imagination.
modalities.whatYouDo: Early sessions are spent describing the house with the therapist: where the child's room is, what breakfast is like, how disagreements are handled and who is home after school. Later, the therapist guides 20-minute scenes of ordinary moments there, and you return to the same rooms each week so that they become familiar.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up in chaotic or unpredictable homes and who long for a sense of order, routine and belonging.
modalities.cautions: Building an ideal home can highlight what your real home lacked and bring up grief or anger, so this is only for work with a therapist who knows childhood trauma and keeps the imagined home clearly separate from memories. Nothing is known yet about whether it helps, so it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: What if you could spend time in a calm, predictable imagined home? The Imagined Home is a new concept: with a therapist you design its rooms, meals and routines, then spend guided time there. For people who grew up in chaos. Untested.

modalities.name: The Asking Hour
modalities.tagline: The questions you never asked as a child, kindly answered.
modalities.whatItIs: The Asking Hour is a hypothetical practice that turns ideal parent imagery into a two-way exchange. In the imagined scene, the child you picture being asks the questions children often carry in silence, such as whether they are too much or why people leave, and the imagined ideal parents answer honestly and kindly.
modalities.coreIdea: Unspoken childhood questions tend to get answered by fear, so this practice gives them a chance to be asked out loud and answered with care.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the imagery, you and a trained therapist choose one question you would have wanted to ask as a child. During a guided scene you ask it, wait and let the imagined parents' answer come, with the therapist stepping in if the answer turns harsh, and afterwards you write the answer down in a sentence or two.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who carry nagging questions about their worth or about relationships, and who like the idea of talking with imagined caregivers, not only receiving from them.
modalities.cautions: Questions like these can lead straight to painful memories, so this belongs only with a licensed therapist experienced in trauma care who keeps the answers clearly imagined, kind and separate from what really happened. It is untested and should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Novel idea: The Asking Hour. In guided imagery, the child you once were finally asks the big questions (am I too much? will you stay?) and imagined ideal parents answer kindly. For people still carrying those questions. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: No Need to Talk
modalities.tagline: Being cared for without having to explain or perform.
modalities.whatItIs: No Need to Talk is a new idea that removes the social effort from ideal parent imagery: you never have to explain, report or be good company. The session follows a fixed sequence, and you respond only with small agreed hand signals while imagined ideal parents care for the child you picture being.
modalities.coreIdea: For people who learned that closeness means performing, being cared for without having to speak or please anyone might be a new experience in itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the first meeting you and a trained therapist agree on the script and on three signals, such as one finger for more, two for slow down and an open hand for stop. In later sessions you sit or lie with eyes closed through a 30-minute guided scene, signaling when needed, with only a brief, optional check-in at the end.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel drained by talking about themselves, who people-please in conversation, or who find the social side of therapy exhausting.
modalities.cautions: With little talking the therapist has less to go on, so it should be done only with a therapist experienced in trauma care who watches closely, and the stop signal must always be honored. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people worn out by talking about themselves: No Need to Talk. A therapist guides imagery of ideal parents caring for the child you once were, and you answer only with hand signals. No explaining, no performing. Untested concept.

modalities.name: Same Scene, Thirty Times
modalities.tagline: One carefully written scene of care, repeated word for word.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Scene, Thirty Times is a speculative idea that pushes ideal parent imagery to the far end of structure. You and a therapist write one short scene of ideal parents caring for the child you picture being, then the therapist guides that exact script, word for word, in about thirty sessions spread over several months.
modalities.coreIdea: Where open, varied experience brings surprise, secure care is partly about sameness, so this practice makes exact repetition the point: the care comes back identical every time.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the first two sessions you and the therapist draft and refine a five-minute script, choosing every word, image and pause. After that, each session opens with the script read in the same voice and pace, followed by a few minutes of rest and a short note on what felt different this time.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up with unpredictable care and who find comfort in routine, ritual and knowing exactly what comes next.
modalities.cautions: Repetition can turn flat or, for some people, stir up memories of rigid or controlling homes, so it should be done only with a therapist experienced in trauma care who can pause or revise the script. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Same Scene, Thirty Times. One short scene of ideal parents caring for the child you once were, written with a therapist and then repeated word for word for months. For people who grew up with unpredictable care. Untested.

modalities.name: Mended Mistake Scenes
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who get it wrong, then make it right.
modalities.whatItIs: Mended Mistake Scenes adds something unusual to ideal parent imagery, a method of picturing care from invented ideal parents: the ideal parents sometimes get things wrong. In planned scenes they are distracted, misunderstand or snap, then notice, apologize and make it right, so the child you picture being learns that a bond can survive mistakes.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure relationships are not perfect ones but ones where breaks get repaired, so this practice rehearses repair rather than flawless care.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist guides structured scenes in three parts: a small, clearly mild misstep by the imagined parents, a pause to notice the hurt, and a warm repair with an apology and a change of course. You rate how safe the relationship feels before and after each repair, and the misstep is always kept small and never resembles real harm.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who experience any conflict or mistake as the end of a relationship, or who cannot forgive themselves or others for small failures.
modalities.cautions: Even mild imagined missteps can echo real hurts, so the scenes must stay small and the work should happen only with a trauma-informed clinician. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: imagery where ideal parents sometimes get it wrong, then apologize and make it right. Mended Mistake Scenes rehearses repair, not perfection. For people who fear any conflict ends a relationship. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Seen With Kind Eyes
modalities.tagline: The quiet experience of being looked at with delight.
modalities.whatItIs: Seen With Kind Eyes is an untested concept that narrows ideal parent imagery down to one silent experience: being looked at with warmth. There is no music, no story and almost no talking, and the scenes center on an imagined ideal parent's face lighting up as they see the child you picture being.
modalities.coreIdea: Much early attunement happens through faces and eyes rather than through words or sound, so this practice concentrates on the quiet experience of being seen and enjoyed.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room, a trained therapist guides a short, structured scene: you picture an ideal parent's face, their eyes finding yours and their expression softening into delight, then you stay with that image in silence for a few minutes. The scene repeats with small variations, such as being seen after a fall or after a success, and ends with a brief check-in.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel invisible, uneasy being looked at, or unsure whether anyone is glad they exist.
modalities.cautions: Being looked at, even in imagination, can feel exposing or stir up memories of cold or angry faces, so this should be done only with a licensed therapist who knows attachment work and keeps it gentle. It has never been tested, so keep any care you already have.
modalities.tweet: For anyone who feels invisible, an untested concept: Seen With Kind Eyes. Quiet guided imagery of an ideal parent's face lighting up when they see the child you once were. No music, no story, just being looked at with warmth. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Inner Siblings
modalities.tagline: Steadier sides of you looking after the younger ones.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Siblings is a proposed twist on parts work, which approaches the mind as a family of inner sides, each with its own feelings and aims. Instead of importing imagined caregivers or relying only on a calm core self, it invites sides of you that are already steadier, such as a capable teenager or a playful ten-year-old, to keep a younger, frightened side company, the way an older sibling might.
modalities.coreIdea: An inner system may already hold its own helpers, so the practice looks for care among the parts themselves rather than bringing any in from outside.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist, you notice a young, distressed side of you and then ask which other sides would be willing to sit with it, checking that each one is calm and kind enough. In loosely guided imagery you let the helper and the young part spend time together, describing what happens without steering it, and the therapist steps in if any helper turns harsh.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find it hard to feel a calm core self, or who sense strength in some sides of themselves but not in others.
modalities.cautions: Helper parts can turn out to be protectors in disguise, and close inner relationships can stir up old family dynamics, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based and trauma work. It is not suitable for people with dissociative conditions, who need specialist care.
modalities.tweet: What if the steadier sides of you could look after the scared ones? Inner Siblings is a new idea for parts work: a capable or playful side keeps a younger, frightened side company, like an older sibling. Untested; only with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Open House for Parts
modalities.tagline: Every side of you may stay, unchanged, as long as it likes.
modalities.whatItIs: Open House for Parts is an untested concept built on one house rule: every side of you is welcome to stay exactly as it is, and none is asked to change, explain itself or remember anything. Where structured therapies test thoughts and set goals, sessions here are open-ended and unhurried, with the therapist acting as co-host to whoever turns up.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts may relax only when they no longer fear being evaluated, corrected or evicted, so the practice offers unconditional residence rather than any plan for change.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session begins by noticing which side of you is present, including any felt in the body, such as a tight jaw or a heavy chest, and simply greeting it. You and the therapist keep it company without questions about its past or its reasons, and if a part starts to tell a painful story, the therapist gently slows things and checks whether it wants to go on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel judged by every approach they have tried, including by their own efforts to improve, and who want a space where nothing about them has to be justified.
modalities.cautions: Open time with inner experience can still bring old pain close, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts and trauma work who takes care not to suggest memories. People with dissociation or in crisis need a more structured, stabilizing approach first.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice: Open House for Parts. One house rule: every side of you may stay exactly as it is, with no need to change, explain or remember. For people who feel judged by every approach they have tried. Untested; only with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Inner Museum
modalities.tagline: Viewing the history of your inner sides as quiet exhibits.
modalities.whatItIs: The Inner Museum is an experimental idea that pushes parts work, the view of the mind as made of many sides, toward history and away from the present moment. Over many sessions you and a therapist imagine a quiet museum in which each side of you has a room showing the era it comes from: what life was like then, what it learned and what it has kept.
modalities.coreIdea: Viewing each side's origins as a respectful exhibit, from the calm distance of a visitor, might let deep history be understood without being relived.
modalities.whatYouDo: With the therapist, you walk through the museum in imagination one room at a time, describing the objects and scenes that come up and checking in with the side of you whose room it is. You never enter a scene, only look at it from the doorway, and each visit ends by closing the room gently and noting what you learned.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who want to understand where their reactions come from and who prefer some distance from painful material.
modalities.cautions: Images of the past can be powerful and are not reliable records of what happened, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work who stops if the distance breaks down. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments for trauma.
modalities.tweet: Concept: The Inner Museum. With a therapist, you imagine a quiet museum where each side of you has a room showing the era it comes from, viewed only from the doorway. For people curious about their past who want some distance from it. Untested.

modalities.name: Parts on a Good Day
modalities.tagline: Getting to know the sides of you that are doing fine.
modalities.whatItIs: Parts on a Good Day is a new idea for parts-based therapy that sets symptoms aside and studies the sides of you that are content, playful, curious or at ease. Instead of hunting for the emotional reasons behind a problem, sessions look at ordinary good moments and ask which sides of you were present and what helped them thrive.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts work usually meets the sides that struggle, so this practice deliberately gets to know the ones that already work well, on the idea that they hold know-how the rest of the system could use.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you bring one recent moment that felt good, even a small one, and a therapist helps you notice the side of you that was there, how it feels in the body and what it enjoys. You ask what it needs to show up more often, and if a worried side interrupts, you acknowledge it and return calmly to the good moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults tired of focusing on what is wrong, or who want to know their strengths from the inside.
modalities.cautions: Turning inward can still stir up harder feelings, and some people feel guilty or uneasy about enjoying good moments, so this should be done only with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Parts on a Good Day. Instead of digging into problems, parts work that gets to know the sides of you that are content, playful or curious, and asks what helps them show up. For people tired of focusing on what's wrong. Therapist-led.

modalities.name: Therapist's Parts Too
modalities.tagline: Client and therapist both name the sides of them that show up.
modalities.whatItIs: Therapist's Parts Too is an invented practice that extends the parts view of the mind to the therapist as well. Carried entirely by conversation, the therapist briefly names their own sides when they show up in a session, such as an eager helper or a worried part, so the meeting becomes one between two inner families rather than one expert and one patient.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing a trusted person notice and steady their own parts in real time might make your own feel less shameful and easier to approach.
modalities.whatYouDo: In ordinary talk-based sessions, the therapist occasionally says something like 'a part of me wants to rush in with advice, so I am going to slow down', always briefly and always handing the focus back to you. Every few sessions you both look at which of your sides tend to set off which of theirs, and agree on what helps.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel inspected in therapy, or who were raised by adults who never admitted their own feelings.
modalities.cautions: Therapist disclosure has to stay brief and serve the client, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based and trauma work, with clear boundaries and supervision. If the therapist's parts start to take up the session, the format should stop.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Therapist's Parts Too. In parts work, the therapist briefly names their own sides too, like 'a part of me wants to rush in with advice', so therapy feels like two people, not an inspection. Untested; only with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Inner Roll Call
modalities.tagline: A brisk check of every known side of you, every session.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Roll Call is a speculative format for parts work that opens every session with a fast, therapist-led roll call of all the sides of you that are already known. Where some methods wait quietly for something to surface, this one takes a quick reading of the whole inner system and lets the result set the session's direction.
modalities.coreIdea: A quick survey of every part may catch the one that most needs attention before it takes over, the way a teacher notices who is missing from class.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist reads out the names you have given your known sides, such as the Planner or the Worried Kid, and you answer for each with one word about how it is doing today. The session then focuses on whichever side sounded loudest, quietest or most changed, and the list grows or shrinks as you get to know your system.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with many competing moods or reactions who like structure and want a clear starting point each week.
modalities.cautions: Naming and checking parts can make them feel more fixed or separate than they are, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work, and it is not suitable for people with dissociative conditions. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Inner Roll Call. Each session opens with a therapist reading the names of the sides of you, the Planner, the Worried Kid, and you answer for each in one word. The loudest or quietest sets the agenda. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Inner Newsletter
modalities.tagline: A weekly written bulletin of what each side of you did.
modalities.whatItIs: The Inner Newsletter is a proposed practice that pushes parts-based therapy toward clear, written differentiation rather than open, undivided presence. Each week you write a one-page newsletter about your inner system, with short items on what each side of you did, said or wanted, and you read it aloud in session.
modalities.coreIdea: Reporting on your sides in a light, journalistic voice might give you a calm, regular overview of patterns that feel confusing from inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: Between sessions you jot quick notes when a side of you shows up, then turn them into short headlines such as 'Critic quiet at work, loud at dinner'. In session the therapist helps you read the newsletter, spot recurring stories and choose one side to get to know better that week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like writing and structure and feel confused by their own mixed reactions.
modalities.cautions: Writing about parts between sessions can stir up feelings when no one is there, so keep it light, stop if it becomes distressing, and use it only within therapy with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is untested, and people with dissociative conditions need specialist care.
modalities.tweet: Idea: The Inner Newsletter. Once a week you write a one-page bulletin about the sides of you, headlines like 'Critic quiet at work, loud at dinner', and read it with your therapist. For people confused by their own mixed reactions. New and untested.

modalities.name: Inner Fire Drill
modalities.tagline: Rehearsing in advance how your inner sides will meet a trigger.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Fire Drill is an untested concept that brings planning and practice to parts work, the opposite of letting things happen. Before a known hard event, such as a family visit, you and a therapist agree what each side of you will do when the trigger hits, rehearse it in imagination like a fire drill, and review afterwards how it went.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts often take over because a trigger catches the system off guard, so agreeing and rehearsing roles in advance might keep the calmer sides in charge when it matters.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a planning session the therapist helps you list which sides usually react to the event and ask each what it would be willing to do instead, such as the angry side signaling early rather than exploding. You rehearse the sequence in imagination two or three times, carry a short written plan to the event, and debrief in the next session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who know their triggers well, such as holidays with family or performance reviews, and want to meet them prepared.
modalities.cautions: Rehearsing triggers can raise distress, and protective sides may resist being given orders, so every role is agreed rather than imposed, and this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. It is untested and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Inner Fire Drill. Before a hard event, like a family holiday, you and a therapist agree what each side of you will do when the trigger hits and rehearse it in imagination. For people who know their triggers and want to be ready.

modalities.name: Grievance Hour for Parts
modalities.tagline: A protected hour for your inner sides to air old complaints.
modalities.whatItIs: Grievance Hour for Parts is a new idea that does the opposite of wishing everyone well: it lets the sides of you speak their grudges, complaints and resentments out loud. Nothing has to be forgiven, resolved or acted on, and the therapist simply helps each grievance be heard in full.
modalities.coreIdea: Resentments that are never voiced can keep parts stuck, so a protected space to complain, without pressure to be kind, might let them loosen in their own time.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a loosely structured session, a therapist invites any side of you with a grievance to speak, whether toward someone in your life, toward another side of you or toward you yourself. You speak for it in the first person, the therapist reflects what it said, and the hour ends with a short settling and a reminder that nothing said needs to be acted on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel they should always be understanding, swallow anger, or carry old resentments they are ashamed of.
modalities.cautions: Voicing anger can stir up strong feelings and painful history, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work, and no grievance should be acted on during or straight after a session. Anyone at risk of harming themselves or others needs specialist help first.
modalities.tweet: Always the understanding one? Grievance Hour for Parts is a new concept: a protected hour where the sides of you air old complaints and grudges out loud, with nothing to forgive or resolve. For people who swallow their anger. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Part Meets Part
modalities.tagline: Seeing your clashes with people as one side meeting another.
modalities.whatItIs: Part Meets Part is a prototype idea that carries the parts view of the mind out into your relationships. Where insight meditation sees experience as impersonal and passing, this practice reads each recurring clash with another person as a very personal meeting: a side of you colliding with a side of them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many arguments repeat because the same two sides keep meeting, so naming both may make room for a calmer side of you to step in next time.
modalities.whatYouDo: You bring a recent clash, such as a fight with your partner about chores, and a therapist helps you notice which side of you reacted and imagine, without mind reading, which side of the other person might have been speaking. You then picture the scene with your calmer self present and plan one different opening line for the next time.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults stuck in repeating conflicts with a partner, parent or colleague who want to understand their own share in them.
modalities.cautions: Guessing at other people's inner sides can turn into blame or labeling, so the focus stays on your own reactions, and this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. In an abusive relationship, the priority is safety, not insight.
modalities.tweet: Same fight, over and over? Part Meets Part is an untested idea: parts work that sees a recurring clash as one side of you meeting one side of them, then plans a different opening line. For people stuck in repeating conflicts. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Whole-System Holiday
modalities.tagline: An imagined trip where no side of you has a job.
modalities.whatItIs: Whole-System Holiday is a speculative idea that takes parts-based therapy to its calmest, least structured end: the whole inner system goes on an imagined holiday together, and every side of you is off duty at once. The worrier does not watch, the planner does not plan, and no one is asked to work on anything.
modalities.coreIdea: Protective sides rarely get a break all at the same time, so imagining a shared holiday might give the system a felt taste of rest without vigilance.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist guides a slow, open-ended scene of the sides of you arriving somewhere peaceful of your choosing, such as a lake, a cabin or a quiet beach, and you simply notice what each one does when it has nothing to do. Any side that will not relax is welcome to stay nearby, and the session ends with a few quiet minutes before you return.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who never feel off duty, find it hard to switch off even on real holidays, or feel tense whenever they rest.
modalities.cautions: For some people, dropping all vigilance at once feels frightening, so no side is pushed to relax, and this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Never feel off duty? A thought experiment: Whole-System Holiday. A therapist guides an imagined trip where every side of you, the worrier, the planner, the critic, gets the day off at once. For people who can't switch off. Untested idea.

modalities.name: Separate Rooms Agreement
modalities.tagline: Inner sides that agree to live apart in peace, not teamwork.
modalities.whatItIs: Separate Rooms Agreement is an untested concept that drops the goal of inner teamwork. Instead of trying to get the sides of you to cooperate or agree, the practice helps them settle into peaceful coexistence, each with its own space, the way housemates who will never be friends can still share a home.
modalities.coreIdea: Some inner conflicts may never resolve, so a quiet agreement to live and let live might bring more peace than pushing for harmony.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist, you work mostly in quiet inner reflection, picturing two or more sides of you that clash and asking each what space it needs and what it wants the other to stop doing. You settle on simple written house rules, such as 'the critic stays out of weekends', and review them every few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults worn out by inner tug-of-wars that never resolve, who would settle for peace instead of agreement.
modalities.cautions: Keeping sides apart should never mean ignoring a part in distress, so the therapist checks that no side is being shut away, and this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is not suitable for people with dissociative conditions, who need specialist care.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Separate Rooms Agreement. Instead of forcing the sides of you to cooperate, you help them live apart in peace, with simple house rules like 'the critic stays out of weekends'. For people tired of inner battles that never end. Untested.

modalities.name: Clean Endings Practice
modalities.tagline: Closing each inner conversation deliberately instead of leaving it open.
modalities.whatItIs: Clean Endings Practice is a proposed form of parts work that pays special attention to stopping. Where steady effort keeps going as long as it can, this practice makes the ending of every inner conversation a careful, deliberate step, so no side of you is left mid-sentence or stirred up.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner work that trails off can leave parts unsettled for days, so learning to close each contact cleanly might make the work feel safer and more contained.
modalities.whatYouDo: In calm, guided sessions, the inner work stops about 15 minutes before the end, and a therapist helps you tell each side you met what will happen next, ask whether it needs anything before you go, and picture it settling somewhere comfortable. Over time you practice the same short closing at home after any strong feeling.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who leave sessions shaken, keep replaying them for days, or find it hard to put feelings down once they are stirred up.
modalities.cautions: Endings can stir up feelings about goodbyes and abandonment, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. It is an untested idea, best kept alongside any care you already receive.
modalities.tweet: Leave therapy shaken and replaying it for days? Concept: Clean Endings Practice. Parts work that saves the last 15 minutes for closing every inner conversation carefully, so no side of you is left stirred up. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Smallest Voice Decides
modalities.tagline: Letting your least powerful inner side choose the direction.
modalities.whatItIs: The Smallest Voice Decides is an experimental idea that turns the usual inner hierarchy upside down. Instead of the strongest, most capable sides of you running things, the quietest, smallest or least powerful side gets to choose what each session is about and when it ends.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner systems are often run by their strongest protectors, so handing the lead to the weakest voice for a while might show what it needs when it is finally allowed to steer.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the start of each loosely structured session, a therapist helps you notice which side of you feels smallest or least heard and asks what it would like to do today, whether that is talking, resting or just being noticed. The more powerful sides are asked to step back and watch, and the therapist checks that they agree.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who are always capable and in control on the outside, and who sense a small, unheard part of themselves underneath.
modalities.cautions: Small, unheard sides often carry old pain, and protectors may push back when sidelined, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work who moves at a gentle pace. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: The Smallest Voice Decides. Parts work where the quietest, least powerful side of you chooses what each session is about, while the capable sides step back. For people always in control on the outside. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Day Planned by Another Part
modalities.tagline: Letting a rarely heard side of you plan an afternoon.
modalities.whatItIs: Day Planned by Another Part is a fresh, untested proposal that gives a rarely heard side of you, such as the playful one, the curious one or the one that wants rest, the chance to plan a few hours of real life. The plan is made in imagination with a therapist, then lived out, then reviewed with that part.
modalities.coreIdea: Some sides of us only ever get a voice in the therapy room, so letting one shape an ordinary afternoon might give it real standing in the system.
modalities.whatYouDo: In session, a therapist helps you find a side of you that rarely gets a say, ask what it would love to do with a free afternoon, and check that your busier sides can allow it. You live that afternoon within safe, simple limits, then report back on how the part and the rest of you felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose lives are run by duty and planning, who sense a playful or restful side that never gets its turn.
modalities.cautions: Plans should stay safe, affordable and legal, and the therapist checks that the chosen side is not a risky urge in disguise; this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: the playful side of you gets to plan your Saturday afternoon. Day Planned by Another Part is an untested idea: plan it with your therapist, live it, then review how it went. For people whose lives run on duty.

modalities.name: Laughing With Parts
modalities.tagline: Gentle, playful humor with the sides of you, never at them.
modalities.whatItIs: Laughing With Parts is a new idea that brings lightness and play into parts work, which sees the mind as many sides with their own aims. Instead of slow, solemn attention, sessions are lively and loosely structured, and you and a therapist find the gentle comedy in your sides, such as a worrier who plans for meteor strikes, always laughing with them and never at them.
modalities.coreIdea: Affectionate humor can soften how harshly we judge our own reactions, so laughing with a part might make it easier to approach than seeing it only as a problem.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist helps you describe one side of you in vivid, exaggerated, affectionate terms, giving it a funny name or catchphrase, and checks that the part enjoys the joke. You then talk with it in that playful spirit about what it is trying to do, and stop the humor at once if any part feels mocked.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with a strong sense of humor who find solemn therapy heavy, or who are very hard on their own quirks.
modalities.cautions: Humor can tip into mockery or be used to dodge real pain, so the therapist watches for both, and this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is untested and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Does your worrier plan for meteor strikes? Laughing With Parts is a new concept: lively parts work that finds the gentle comedy in the sides of you, always laughing with them, never at them. For people who find solemn therapy heavy. Untested.

modalities.name: Inner Shift Rota
modalities.tagline: Mapping which sides of you are on duty, and when.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Shift Rota is a speculative idea that looks at the sides of you as a workforce on shifts. In quiet, structured sessions, you and a therapist work out which side tends to be on duty at different times, such as the planner in the morning or the worrier after midnight, and then redesign the rota.
modalities.coreIdea: Many difficult hours may come from the wrong side working the wrong shift, so arranging who is on duty when might ease pressure without anyone having to change completely.
modalities.whatYouDo: For two weeks you note briefly which side of you seemed in charge at a few set times each day, and in session the therapist helps you lay these notes out as a weekly rota. You then ask the sides involved whether they would swap or shorten shifts, for example letting a restful side take the late evening, and check the new rota after a fortnight.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose moods follow strong daily patterns, such as dread on Sunday nights or worry in the small hours.
modalities.cautions: Daily patterns of low mood or sleeplessness can have medical causes worth checking with a doctor, and this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is untested, and people with dissociative conditions need specialist care.
modalities.tweet: Is your worrier working the night shift? Inner Shift Rota is a new idea: map which sides of you are on duty at which hours, then work with a therapist to swap a few shifts. For people with Sunday-night dread or small-hours worry. Untested.

modalities.name: Parts Interview You
modalities.tagline: Your wary inner sides question you before they trust you.
modalities.whatItIs: Parts Interview You is an untested concept that reverses the usual direction of parts work. Instead of you asking a protective side about its job, the wary sides of you interview you, the adult in charge, about whether you can be trusted with what they guard, in a structured, step-by-step format with a therapist.
modalities.coreIdea: Protectors may hold back because they doubt the adult self is up to the job, so giving them a formal chance to question it might build trust on their terms.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist helps a protective side of you write a short list of questions for you, such as 'what will you do if we stop watching', and then you answer each one in session while the part listens. The part rates its trust after each answer and says what would raise it, and the interview resumes a few weeks later.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose protective habits refuse to budge and who suspect part of them simply does not trust them yet.
modalities.cautions: Hard questions from wary parts can stir up shame or pressure, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work who keeps the pace gentle. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: What if your wary inner sides got to interview you before trusting you? Parts Interview You is a new concept: protective parts ask the adult you hard questions and rate their trust. For people whose habits refuse to budge. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Inner Casting Call
modalities.tagline: Casting each side of you as a character from a story.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Casting Call is an experimental idea that gives each side of you a vivid character to play. Instead of attending to raw sensation, you and a therapist cast your sides with characters from films, books or myths, such as a nervous sidekick or a stern headteacher, and use their stories to understand how those sides act.
modalities.coreIdea: A familiar character can capture a side of you faster and more kindly than a clinical description, and its story might suggest new roles that side could grow into.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each session you describe one side of you and try out characters until one feels right, then talk with the therapist about what that character is like at its best and at its worst. You imagine how the character would handle a current situation differently, and over time you may recast a side as it changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who love films and stories and find it easier to understand themselves through characters.
modalities.cautions: Fictional labels can stick and make a side seem more fixed than it is, so keep the casting light, and use it only within therapy with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is untested and not suitable for people with dissociative conditions.
modalities.tweet: Who would play your inner critic in a film? Inner Casting Call is an untested idea: with a therapist you cast each side of you as a character, a nervous sidekick, a stern headteacher, and learn from their stories. For lovers of films and books.

modalities.name: One Part per Month
modalities.tagline: A whole quiet month devoted to one side of you.
modalities.whatItIs: One Part per Month is a proposed format for parts work that trades breadth for depth and quiet steadiness. For a whole month, all sessions and a daily one-minute check-in are devoted to a single side of you, with no other parts explored and nothing louder allowed to take over.
modalities.coreIdea: Attention that keeps jumping between parts may never let any one of them feel truly known, so a month of steady, quiet focus on one side might build a deeper relationship.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the start of the month you and a therapist choose one side of you, ideally a manageable one such as the planner or the shy one. Each day you spend a minute noticing how it is, each weekly session goes deeper with it, and if other sides demand attention you note them for a later month.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel scattered in therapy, or who prefer slow, steady, focused work.
modalities.cautions: A month of focus can bring up more than expected, especially with sides linked to old hurts, so start with a manageable side and work only with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Feel scattered in therapy? Concept: One Part per Month. A whole month of sessions, plus a daily one-minute check-in, devoted to a single side of you, so it can be known properly. For people who like slow, steady work. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Study of One
modalities.tagline: Running a proper, planned study with yourself as the subject.
modalities.whatItIs: Study of One is a new, unproven idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) further into the present and the real world than it usually goes. Instead of exploring the past or testing single thoughts, you run a planned study of your own life, switching one everyday change on and off for set weeks and rating your mood each day to see what actually makes a difference.
modalities.coreIdea: General advice may not fit you, so the practice turns you into a careful researcher of your own life, using the logic of a controlled trial.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach, you pick one change, such as no screens after 10 pm or a morning walk, and plan four two-week blocks that alternate with and without it. Each evening you rate mood, sleep and energy in an app or notebook, and at the end the coach helps you compare the blocks and decide what to keep.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like data, distrust one-size-fits-all advice, and want to find out what helps them specifically.
modalities.cautions: Never stop or change medication as part of a self-study, and talk to a doctor before changing sleep, diet or exercise if you have a health condition. Severe low mood or suicidal thoughts call for professional help, not a study.
modalities.tweet: Be your own research lab. Study of One is a new concept: switch one everyday change on and off in two-week blocks, rate your mood daily, and see what really helps you. For people who distrust one-size-fits-all advice. Untested; never change medication for it.

modalities.name: Calm-Day Constitution
modalities.tagline: Rules you write when calm, to guide you when you are not.
modalities.whatItIs: Calm-Day Constitution is a speculative idea that takes the structure of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward self-governance. Rather than hearing out the different sides of you that pull each way, you act as one lawmaker: on a calm day you write a short constitution of standing decisions for heated moments, and it can only be amended by a set procedure.
modalities.coreIdea: Decisions made in distress are often the ones we regret, so the practice lets your calm self set guidelines in advance and makes changing them slow on purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach or therapist, you draft about ten articles, such as 'I never send an angry message until the next morning' or 'I do not quit a job in the same week I want to'. When a heated moment comes you follow the article, and any change must be written down, wait a week and be agreed in a session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who act on impulse in heated moments and later regret it, and who like clear commitments.
modalities.cautions: Articles must stay kind and flexible enough for real emergencies, and they should never stop you from seeking help or leaving an unsafe situation. Strong impulsivity linked to mood swings, substance use or self-harm needs a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: What if your calm self could write rules for your stressed self? Calm-Day Constitution is a new idea: write ten standing decisions on a good day, follow them in heated moments, and amend them only after a week's wait. For impulsive regretters. Untested.

modalities.name: Feeling on Cue
modalities.tagline: Practicing calling up chosen feelings on purpose.
modalities.whatItIs: Feeling on Cue is an untested concept that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) as far as it goes toward deliberate change, the reverse of simply making room for feelings. With a therapist, you build a small repertoire of feelings you would like to reach more often, such as calm confidence or warm interest, and practice calling each one up on purpose with prepared thoughts and images.
modalities.coreIdea: If thoughts shape feelings, then calling up a helpful feeling might be a trainable skill, practiced on cue until it becomes more reliable.
modalities.whatYouDo: For each target feeling, you and the therapist write a short script of thoughts, memories and images that tend to bring it on, then you practice it in session and rate how strongly the feeling arrives. Between sessions you rehearse once a day and before situations where that feeling would help, such as calm confidence before a meeting.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel at the mercy of their moods and want an active, practical way to steer them.
modalities.cautions: This is about adding feelings, not pushing away painful ones, so if it turns into suppressing grief, fear or anger, stop and talk it through with the therapist. Persistent low mood or anxiety needs a full assessment by a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Could feelings be called up on cue, like a skill? Feeling on Cue is a new concept: with a therapist you write scripts that bring on chosen feelings, like calm confidence, and practice until they come more reliably. For people at the mercy of moods. Untested.

modalities.name: Day Zero Mornings
modalities.tagline: Planning each day as if your history did not decide it.
modalities.whatItIs: Day Zero Mornings is an experimental idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) fully into the present, the opposite of tracing problems to their roots. Each morning you plan the day with a short checklist that rules out reasons from the past, such as 'I always fail at this', and asks only what you would choose to do today if you were starting fresh.
modalities.coreIdea: Stories about who we have always been can quietly decide each day for us, so a structured daily fresh start might loosen that momentum.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every morning for five minutes you answer the same four written questions, such as 'what would a fresh-start version of me do first today', and pick one action. In the evening you note only how today went, without comparing it to the past, and every week or two you review the notebook with a coach.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel trapped by their track record, or who keep repeating patterns because 'that is just who I am'.
modalities.cautions: This is a daily exercise, not a way to ignore real history: past trauma, debts or health problems still need proper attention. If old memories keep pushing in, that is a sign to work with a clinician rather than to push harder.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Day Zero Mornings. Each morning a five-minute checklist asks what you'd do today if your history didn't decide it, with no 'I always fail at this' allowed. For people who feel trapped by their track record.

modalities.name: Teacher's Turn
modalities.tagline: Learning thinking skills by preparing to teach them to others.
modalities.whatItIs: Teacher's Turn is a proposed group format that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward learning by teaching, carried entirely by talk. In a small facilitated group, members take turns preparing and teaching one practical thinking skill to the others, using examples from imagined everyday situations.
modalities.coreIdea: People often understand and remember a skill best when they have to explain it to someone else, so the practice turns every member into a teacher.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of five to seven meet weekly for 90 minutes, and each week one or two members give a ten-minute lesson on a skill the facilitator assigned, such as spotting all-or-nothing thinking. The others try the skill on a made-up example and give friendly feedback, and the teacher then applies it to their own week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who learn best by explaining, enjoy helping others, or feel more confident in a teaching role.
modalities.cautions: Teaching in front of a group can feel exposing, so lessons are short, feedback rules are strict and anyone can pass, and the facilitator should be a trained clinician. People in crisis or with severe social anxiety may need individual support first.
modalities.tweet: Best way to learn something? Teach it. Teacher's Turn is a new concept: in a small group, members take turns giving ten-minute lessons on a thinking skill, then try it on their own week. For people who learn by explaining. Untested; with a trained facilitator.

modalities.name: Thinking Out Loud Transcripts
modalities.tagline: Recording your thinking aloud, then studying the transcript together.
modalities.whatItIs: Thinking Out Loud Transcripts is a thought experiment that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward close, explicit analysis, the opposite of waiting for a vague bodily sense to become clear. You record yourself thinking aloud about a problem for five minutes, then you and a therapist study a written transcript of it.
modalities.coreIdea: How we think may be easier to see on the page than from inside, so the practice makes your own spoken thinking a text to be read closely.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you record one five-minute ramble about something on your mind and turn it into text with a transcription app. In session, you and the therapist mark patterns, such as how often you ask questions you never answer, jump to the future or repeat the same phrase, and you pick one pattern to experiment with in next week's recording.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who overthink, like analysis and writing, and want to see their thinking habits clearly.
modalities.cautions: Reading your own worries in print can be uncomfortable or feed self-criticism, so the therapist keeps the tone curious and kind. Keep recordings private and stored securely, and get a full assessment if worry is constant or overwhelming.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Thinking Out Loud Transcripts. Record yourself thinking aloud for five minutes, then read the transcript with a therapist and spot your habits, like questions you never answer. For overthinkers who like analysis. Untested.

modalities.name: Skill Belt Grading
modalities.tagline: Earning colored belts in practical mental skills, like a martial art.
modalities.whatItIs: Skill Belt Grading is a speculative idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward clear, graded performance, the opposite of open-ended unfolding. Practical mental skills, from noticing a thought to planning a hard conversation, are arranged into belts like a martial art, each with a short practical test.
modalities.coreIdea: Visible stages and earned milestones may keep people practicing skills that otherwise fade, and turn progress into something you can see.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach, you start at the first belt, which might cover noticing and naming feelings, and practice its three skills for a few weeks. To pass, you show each skill in a short live test, such as calming yourself after a stressful role-play, and then move on to the next belt.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like goals, levels and clear progress, and who lose motivation when improvement feels invisible.
modalities.cautions: Grading can feed perfectionism or shame, so failing a test only means practicing longer, and belts are never compared between people. Low motivation can be a sign of depression, which needs proper assessment and care rather than more tests.
modalities.tweet: Mental skills, graded like a martial art. Skill Belt Grading is an untested idea: earn belts in practical skills, from naming feelings to handling hard talks, each with a short live test. For people who lose motivation when progress feels invisible.

modalities.name: Mission Control Day
modalities.tagline: A small group plans and supports one member's hard day.
modalities.whatItIs: Mission Control Day is an untested concept that brings maximum planning and support to a single difficult day. A facilitated group acts as mission control for one member: together they plan the day hour by hour, agree on checkpoints, and send brief check-in messages at set times while it happens.
modalities.coreIdea: A hard day may feel more manageable when it is planned in detail and you know people are following along, so the practice borrows the structure of a space mission.
