modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of five or six meet weekly, and each session one member presents an upcoming hard day, such as a job interview or a court date, and the group plans it with checkpoints and backup plans. On the day, members send short messages at the agreed times, and the next session starts with a debrief.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults facing a specific, dreaded day who feel alone with it and do better with a clear plan and company.
modalities.cautions: Messages and plans involve personal details, so the group agrees strict privacy rules, members choose what to share, and the facilitator should be a trained clinician. A real emergency always goes to emergency services, not the group.
modalities.tweet: Facing a dreaded day? Mission Control Day is a new concept: a small facilitated group plans your day hour by hour, sets checkpoints, and sends short check-in messages while it happens. For people who feel alone with a hard day. Untested.

modalities.name: The Honest Survey
modalities.tagline: Checking beliefs about how others see you against real answers.
modalities.whatItIs: The Honest Survey is a hypothetical practice that swaps warm wishes for cool data. Where loving-kindness practice quietly sends goodwill to others, this practice asks real people in your life, through a short anonymous survey designed with a therapist, how they actually see you on the points you worry about most.
modalities.coreIdea: Beliefs such as 'everyone finds me boring' are rarely checked against what people really think, so careful, anonymous questions might replace guesswork with evidence.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist you write five neutral questions, such as 'how easy is this person to talk to, from 1 to 5', and send them through an anonymous form to eight to twelve people who know you. You predict the answers beforehand, then read the results together with the therapist in session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with strong worries about how others see them who are ready to look at real answers with support.
modalities.cautions: Answers can sting, so questions are kept neutral and specific, results are read only in session with the therapist, and people with severe social anxiety or depression should wait until they feel steadier. Respondents' anonymity must be protected.
modalities.tweet: Worried everyone finds you boring? The Honest Survey is an untested idea: with a therapist you write five neutral questions, send them anonymously to people who know you, and compare the answers with your predictions. For people ready for real data.

modalities.name: Crossroads Play Night
modalities.tagline: A group board game where life situations meet coping choices.
modalities.whatItIs: Crossroads Play Night is a proposed group practice that turns CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) skills into a board game, the opposite of quietly watching experience pass. Players move through imagined everyday situations, such as a turned-down invitation or a missed deadline, and choose how to think and act at each crossroads, earning points for flexible, workable choices.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing choices in a playful, imagined setting might make new responses feel familiar before they are needed in real life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to six players meet weekly for 90 minutes with a facilitator, drawing situation cards and debating possible responses before each player picks one and explains it. After the game, each player chooses one crossroads that resembles their own week and plans how to try that choice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who learn through play, enjoy games and discussion, or find direct self-examination heavy.
modalities.cautions: Situation cards can hit close to home, so anyone can skip a card, and the facilitator should be a trained clinician. Games can turn competitive, so points reward flexibility rather than right answers.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Crossroads Play Night. A small group plays through imagined everyday situations, like a turned-down invitation, choosing how to think and act at each crossroads and scoring points for flexible choices. For people who learn through play.

modalities.name: Season Review Sessions
modalities.tagline: Long, calm sessions every three months to see slow patterns.
modalities.whatItIs: Season Review Sessions is an experimental idea that slows CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) right down, the opposite of short, intense bursts. Instead of weekly sessions, you meet a therapist once every three months for a long, calm, structured review of the whole season, looking for patterns that only show over months.
modalities.coreIdea: Some thinking habits move too slowly to notice week to week, so stepping back to a seasonal timescale might reveal them clearly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each review you fill in a simple monthly sheet on mood, sleep, stress and key events, and the three-hour session starts with relaxation, then lays the months out on a timeline. Together you mark recurring dips and recoveries, name the thoughts that came with them and set one small aim for the next season.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with slow, recurring patterns, such as winter lows or yearly work crunches, or who cannot attend weekly therapy.
modalities.cautions: Three months is a long gap, so you need a clear plan for getting help sooner if things worsen, and it is not suitable during a crisis. Seasonal low mood that is severe deserves a medical assessment.
modalities.tweet: Some patterns only show over months. Season Review Sessions is a new idea: one long, calm session every three months to lay the season out on a timeline and spot slow cycles, like winter lows. For people who can't do weekly therapy. Untested.

modalities.name: Attention Budget
modalities.tagline: Budgeting the minutes your mind spends worrying, replaying and planning.
modalities.whatItIs: Attention Budget is a new idea that runs CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) as quiet, solitary bookkeeping of the mind. You estimate how many minutes a day go to worrying, replaying the past, planning and simply being present, then set a monthly budget for each, the way you might budget money.
modalities.coreIdea: Attention is limited, and seeing where it goes in plain numbers might make it easier to spend more of it on purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: For two weeks you make a quick estimate three times a day of what your mind has mostly been doing, and a therapist helps you total it into a monthly statement. You then agree on budgets, such as no more than 30 minutes of replaying a day, and note simple ways to spend less, such as a five-minute walk when the replay budget runs out.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel their minds run away with them, like numbers and tracking, and prefer working quietly on their own between sessions.
modalities.cautions: Tracking can become another source of self-criticism, so estimates stay rough and overspending counts as information, not failure. Constant worry or rumination may be a sign of anxiety or depression that needs a full assessment.
modalities.tweet: Where does your mind's time go? Attention Budget is an untested concept: track rough minutes spent worrying, replaying and planning, then set a monthly budget for each, like money. For people whose minds run away with them. With a therapist's support.

modalities.name: Done in the Room
modalities.tagline: All the practice happens live, with no homework at all.
modalities.whatItIs: Done in the Room proposes removing homework from CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) and doing all the practice together with the therapist during sessions. Where most CBT asks you to practice alone between visits, here the therapist leads every exercise live, step by step, so nothing depends on stamina or willpower at home.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people cannot keep up practice alone, so moving all of it into longer guided sessions might make the method usable for them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sessions last about two hours, once or twice a week, and each one includes a full practice block led by the therapist, such as filling in a worksheet together or making a hard phone call while the therapist sits beside you. You leave with no tasks, only a short summary of what you did.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who have dropped out of therapy because of homework, live in chaotic circumstances, or find it hard to get started on their own.
modalities.cautions: Longer sessions can be tiring and costly, and some skills may fade without practice at home, so progress in this untested format should be reviewed regularly. Severe depression or suicidal thoughts call for prompt professional help.
modalities.tweet: Hated therapy homework? Concept: Done in the Room. All the practice happens live in longer sessions with your therapist, from worksheets to that dreaded phone call, so nothing depends on willpower at home. For people who can't self-start. Untested.

modalities.name: Subtraction Weeks
modalities.tagline: Removing one obligation a week instead of trying harder.
modalities.whatItIs: Subtraction Weeks is a speculative idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward lightening the load rather than building more strength to carry it. Each week, with a therapist's help, you list your commitments, weigh what each costs and gives, and remove or shrink exactly one.
modalities.coreIdea: Stress often comes from the sheer number of demands rather than a lack of coping skills, so steady subtraction might do more than another self-improvement plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the first session you write down every regular commitment, from work duties to group chats and favors, and score each for energy cost and value. Each week you pick one to drop, delegate or shrink, predict what will happen, and report back on what actually did.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel overloaded and keep adding coping strategies instead of reducing demands.
modalities.cautions: Some duties, such as caring for children or legal obligations, cannot simply be dropped, so subtraction focuses on what is truly optional. Overload with exhaustion or low mood may also need medical care.
modalities.tweet: Overloaded? Instead of trying harder, Subtraction Weeks is a new idea: each week, with a therapist, you weigh your commitments and drop or shrink exactly one, then see what really happens. For people who keep adding instead of removing. Untested.

modalities.name: Puzzle Circuit Breaker
modalities.tagline: Breaking rumination loops with a demanding mental task.
modalities.whatItIs: Puzzle Circuit Breaker is an untested concept that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward cool, effortful thinking as a way out of worry, the opposite of seeking comfort. When a rumination loop starts, you switch to a short, demanding mental task, such as a number puzzle or memory game, chosen in advance to fully occupy the mind.
modalities.coreIdea: Rumination needs mental space, so a puzzle hard enough to use all of it might break the loop long enough for a calmer next step.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist or coach, you choose three puzzles that fully absorb you, test them in session and set a rule, such as ten minutes of puzzle once you notice you have replayed the same thought three times. You log whether the loop returned and what you did afterwards, and review the log every week or two.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who get stuck replaying worries or arguments and like puzzles, games or mental challenges.
modalities.cautions: Puzzles are a pause button, not a way to avoid real problems, so pair each break with a plan for dealing with what the worry is about. Rumination that fills most of the day may be a sign of depression or anxiety that needs a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Stuck in a worry loop? Puzzle Circuit Breaker is a new concept: when the same thought comes round three times, switch to a puzzle hard enough to use your whole mind for ten minutes. For ruminators who love games. Untested, and no way to dodge problems.

modalities.name: Forecasters' League
modalities.tagline: Scoring how well you predict your own days, as a group.
modalities.whatItIs: Forecasters' League is an invented practice that turns CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) into a brisk prediction game played in a small group. Each member makes daily forecasts about their own life, such as 'the meeting will go badly, 80 percent sure', and the league scores how well calibrated each person's forecasts turn out to be.
modalities.coreIdea: Anxious and gloomy forecasts are rarely scored, so keeping a running score of your own predictions might show how far your inner forecaster can be trusted.
modalities.whatYouDo: Members log three forecasts a day with a confidence level in a shared app or notebook, then record what happened. At weekly meetings, a facilitator shows each person's calibration chart and the group discusses which kinds of forecasts tend to run too dark or too bright.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who worry about the future, enjoy games and numbers, and like friendly competition.
modalities.cautions: Scores can feel like judgments, so the league rewards better calibration rather than optimism, and members can keep their charts private. Persistent dread or hopelessness needs a full assessment by a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Picture a league for forecasting your own life. Forecasters' League is an untested idea: log daily predictions, like 'the meeting will go badly, 80% sure', and see how well calibrated you are. For worriers who love numbers and friendly competition.

modalities.name: Own Yardstick Practice
modalities.tagline: Measuring yourself against your own past, not other people.
modalities.whatItIs: Own Yardstick Practice is a new idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) away from the social world in one specific way: it retires other people as your measuring stick. With a therapist planning each step, you notice when you compare yourself with others and systematically swap in a comparison with your own past.
modalities.coreIdea: Comparing yourself with other people's highlights rarely ends well, so a fixed personal yardstick might give a fairer and steadier sense of progress.
modalities.whatYouDo: For a month you note each comparison with someone else, then answer two set questions in its place: how you are doing compared with a year ago, and what one small step would move you on. In weekly sessions the therapist reviews the log and helps you build a simple chart of your own progress.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who constantly measure themselves against friends, colleagues or social media and come off worse.
modalities.cautions: Looking back at your own past can be painful if it held loss or illness, so the therapist helps choose comparison points carefully. Comparison that drives disordered eating, severe low mood or self-harm needs a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Always coming off worse next to other people? Own Yardstick Practice is an untested concept: catch each comparison and swap in one question, how am I doing compared with a year ago? For people stuck on social media scorecards. With a therapist.

modalities.name: Rooms of Reminders
modalities.tagline: Storing coping thoughts in an imagined building you can walk through.
modalities.whatItIs: Rooms of Reminders is an untested concept that borrows the memory palace, an old memorization method, for CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy). With a therapist guiding each step, you place your most useful coping thoughts in the rooms of a building you know well, so they can be found again under stress by walking through it in your mind.
modalities.coreIdea: Helpful thoughts are easy to forget when you are upset, and linking them to vivid imagined places might make them easier to recall when they matter.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a familiar building, such as your old school or your flat, and the therapist helps you place one coping thought in each room as a striking image, such as a lifeguard by the bathtub for 'I have handled this before'. You rehearse the walk in session and daily for a few weeks, then use it in stressful moments and report back.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with a good visual imagination who know helpful thoughts in theory but lose them when stressed.
modalities.cautions: Choose a building with neutral or happy associations, since one tied to painful memories can stir them up. Imagery works best as one tool among several, and strong distress or panic needs a fuller plan with a clinician.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Rooms of Reminders. With a therapist, you store your best coping thoughts in the rooms of an imagined building, like a lifeguard by the bathtub for 'I've handled this before', and walk through it when stressed. Untested.

modalities.name: Next Chapter Circle
modalities.tagline: A group co-writes a character's story, one new chapter a week.
modalities.whatItIs: Next Chapter Circle is a proposed group practice that leaves raw sensation behind for imagination and story. In a small facilitated group, members co-write a weekly serialized story about an invented character who meets challenges like their own and, chapter by chapter, tries new ways of thinking and acting.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing new responses for a character might be a low-pressure rehearsal of the scripts you want for yourself, with the group as co-authors and audience.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 90-minute session starts with the latest chapter read aloud, then the group discusses where the character is stuck and pitches what they might try next. One or two members draft the next chapter at home, and each session ends with members privately noting one move from the story to try that week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who love stories and writing and who find it easier to imagine change for a character than for themselves.
modalities.cautions: Stories can hit close to home, so members can always pass or step out, and the facilitator should be a trained clinician who checks in with anyone upset. People in crisis need individual professional help rather than a group.
modalities.tweet: Experimental idea: Next Chapter Circle. A small group co-writes a weekly story about an invented character facing challenges like theirs, trying new moves chapter by chapter. For people who find it easier to imagine change for someone else. Untested.

modalities.name: Your Own Dictionary
modalities.tagline: Writing precise definitions for the loaded words you judge yourself with.
modalities.whatItIs: Your Own Dictionary is a speculative idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward plain, exact language and away from expression and mood. With a therapist, you write dictionary-style definitions for the loaded words you use about yourself, such as failure, lazy or selfish, with clear criteria for when each really applies.
modalities.coreIdea: Words like failure often carry no definition at all, so pinning down exactly what they mean might show how rarely they fit.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you choose one word you often use against yourself and draft a definition with examples of what does and does not count, then the therapist helps you test it against real people and situations. Over a few months you build a short personal dictionary you can check whenever the word comes up.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with harsh labels for themselves who like precision, language and logic.
modalities.cautions: Defining painful words can bring up shame, so the work moves slowly and stays kind. Harsh self-labeling linked to depression or suicidal thoughts needs prompt professional help.
modalities.tweet: What does 'lazy' actually mean? Your Own Dictionary is a new idea: with a therapist, you write precise definitions, with criteria, for the harsh words you use about yourself. For people who like precision and logic. Untested.
